title: Writing practice: Fact sheets, prices, weather, and stories
description: Eight writing tasks: write from a fact sheet, argue about the fastest typist, explain a sea breeze, and retell a story from one character's point of view.

stimuli.title: Maple Street Community Garden: fact sheet
stimuli.caption: Facts about a community garden that the school newsletter will describe.
rows: Behind the public library on Maple Street
Students and neighbors, every Saturday morning
Shared with families and a local food pantry

stimuli.title: Three typing tests
stimuli.caption: Three students each typed for a different number of minutes. The table shows how many words each student typed.

stimuli.title: A beach at noon on a sunny day
stimuli.caption: Temperatures were measured at the same time in four places on a beach. Scientists know that sand heats up faster than water in sunshine, and that warm air rises. When air moves in to replace rising air, we feel a wind.

stimuli.title: Orange sales at Harbor Market
stimuli.caption: A frost damaged many orange trees in November. The number of shoppers who wanted oranges stayed about the same each month.
columns: Bags of oranges delivered to the market

stimuli.title: Class blog: How We Learn
paragraphs: Your class is making a blog called “How We Learn.” Each student writes a short story about one time they learned something new, at school, at home, or in the community.
Think about these questions: What did you want to learn? Who or what helped you? What happened first, next, and last? What can you do now?

stimuli.title: Read: The Watch on the Bench
paragraphs: Every morning, Tobias swept the floor of the clock shop while Mr. Okafor repaired tiny gears at his bench. Tobias wanted to repair clocks too, but Mr. Okafor only said, “Not yet.”

One afternoon, a customer brought in a pocket watch that had stopped. Mr. Okafor was out delivering a clock, and the customer needed the watch that day. Tobias took a deep breath, opened the case with the smallest screwdriver, and found a bent spring. He straightened it carefully and closed the case.

When Mr. Okafor returned, he held the watch to his ear and raised his eyebrows. “Who did this?” Tobias admitted it, expecting to be scolded. Instead, Mr. Okafor handed him a pair of tweezers. “Tomorrow,” he said, “you sit at the bench with me.”

stimuli.title: Bean plants and daily water
stimuli.caption: Five groups of bean plants were grown for three weeks. Each group received a different amount of water every day. All groups had the same soil, light, and temperature. The table shows the average height of the plants in each group. Plant roots take in oxygen from air spaces in the soil. Very wet soil has fewer air spaces.

stimuli.title: The old train station: keep it or replace it?
stimuli.caption: A city must decide what to do with its old train station. The table gives facts about each choice. Students in your class will vote on what young people think.
rows: Built in 1912; visitors come from other cities to see it; repairs cost $2 million
The apartments would give homes to about 200 families; building costs $5 million; the old building would be gone

items.stem: Write an informational paragraph for the school newsletter about the Maple Street Community Garden. Use the facts in the table.

checklist: I began with a topic sentence that tells what the garden is.
I included at least four facts from the table.
I wrote in my own words and did not copy whole rows.
I ended with a concluding sentence.
exemplar: Topic sentence identifies the subject and the purpose
Presents at least four facts accurately (location, 24 beds, crops, who works there, where the food goes)
Groups related information and uses noun groups (for example, fresh vegetables and herbs)
Uses present tense and simple connectors (and, also, because)
Closing sentence says why the garden matters

support.clue: Read each row of the table. Choose four rows. Think about how to put them in an order that makes sense: where it is, what it has, who works there, and what happens to the food.
support.frame: The Maple Street Community Garden is ______. It has ______. In the garden, people grow ______. ______ work there on ______. The food is ______. This garden is important because ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different place. “The Riverside Skate Park is a place for young people to practice. It has three ramps and a smooth floor. Skaters of all ages visit on weekends. The park is free to use. It is important because it gives people a safe place to exercise.” Notice the topic sentence, the facts, and the closing idea. Write about the garden the same way.

facts: All garden details are fictional facts supplied in the table: Maple Street location, 24 beds, crops, Saturday volunteers, sharing with families and a food pantry.

items.stem: Dev says, “Ben is the fastest typist because he typed the most words.” Do you agree or disagree? Write an argument that uses the number of words each student typed in one minute.

checklist: I said whether I agree or disagree with Dev.
I showed how I found the words typed in one minute for each student.
I compared the three rates and named the fastest typist.
I explained why typing the most words does not always mean typing the fastest.
exemplar: Takes a clear position and disagrees with Dev
Finds the rate for each student correctly: Ana 30 words per minute, Ben 25 words per minute, Cai 35 words per minute
Compares the three rates to identify Cai as the fastest typist
Explains that the most words in total does not mean the fastest, because the students typed for different numbers of minutes
Uses mathematical language (divide, per minute, rate) and connectors accurately

support.clue: The students typed for different numbers of minutes, so the totals are hard to compare. What could you divide to find the words typed in one minute?
support.frame: I disagree with Dev because ______. To find the words typed in one minute, I divide ______ by ______. Ana types ______ words per minute, Ben types ______, and Cai types ______. Therefore, ______ is the fastest typist. Although Ben ______, ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different comparison. “I disagree with Lea that Test 1 was the better score because I got more answers right. On Test 1, I got 21 of 30 right, which is 70%. On Test 2, I got 18 of 24 right, which is 75%. Therefore, Test 2 was the better score even though I got fewer answers right.” Notice the position, the calculation, and the comparison. Make your argument about the typing tests the same way.

facts: Cai types the most words per minute, although Ben typed the most words in total (200).

items.stem: People at this beach feel a cool wind blowing from the sea onto the land. Explain what causes this wind. Use the temperatures in the table and describe each step in the process.

checklist: I used the temperatures to show which place is warmer.
I described the steps in order: heating, rising, and moving in.
I used cause-and-effect words such as because, so, and as a result.
I used science words such as air, rise, and temperature.
exemplar: Identifies the temperature difference between the air above the sand (33°C) and the air above the water (26°C)
Sequences the chain: sand heats the air, warm air rises, cooler air from over the water moves in to replace it, which is the wind
States the direction of the wind (from the sea to the land)
Uses causal connectors and scientific vocabulary precisely

support.clue: Compare the air above the sand with the air above the water. Which air is warmer? Then think about what warm air does and what must take its place.
support.frame: The sand is ______ than the water, so ______. Because warm air ______, ______. As a result, a wind blows from ______ to ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different process. “When it rains on a flat road, the water cannot soak into the hard ground. Because the road is lower in the middle, the water runs to the low place. Then more water collects there. As a result, a puddle forms.” Notice the steps in order and the connecting words. Explain how the beach wind forms the same way.

facts: Land and sand heat up faster than water in sunlight.
Cooler air moves in to replace rising warm air, which produces wind.
During the day, a sea breeze blows from the sea toward the land.

items.stem: Write an explanation for a classmate who is studying economics. Explain why the price of oranges went up in November and why it came down again by January. Use the words supply and demand, and describe the chain of causes and effects.

checklist: I explained the cause of the price change in November.
I used the words supply and demand correctly.
I used numbers from the table as evidence.
I explained why the price fell again in January.
I used cause-and-effect connectors to link my ideas.
exemplar: Names the frost as the first cause and the drop in supply (500 to 250 bags) as its effect
Explains that demand stayed about the same, so shoppers competed for fewer bags and the price rose to $7
Uses supply and demand accurately as academic vocabulary
Explains the recovery: supply returned to about 480 bags, so the price fell to $4.25
Sustains the causal chain with varied connectors and uses specific data from the table

support.clue: Look at how the number of bags changed from October to November and how the price changed. Which word names the amount available to sell? Which word names how much people want to buy?
support.frame: The frost damaged ______, so the supply of oranges ______. Because demand ______, ______. As a result, the price ______ from ______ to ______. By January, ______. Consequently, ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different market. “A new bakery opened next to a school, so the supply of fresh bread increased from 100 loaves to 300 loaves a day. Because the number of customers stayed the same, the bakery had many loaves left over. As a result, it lowered the price from $5 to $3 to attract buyers. Consequently, more families bought bread.” Notice the cause, the effect on supply, the effect on price, and the result. Explain the orange market the same way.

facts: When supply falls and demand stays about the same, prices tend to rise.
When supply recovers, prices tend to fall.
Market figures are given in the table (invented data): 500 bags at $4, 250 bags at $7, 480 bags at $4.25.

items.stem: Write your blog story about a time you learned something new. Tell what happened in order.

checklist: I told what I wanted to learn.
I told what happened in order, using words like first, next, and finally.
I used past-tense verbs.
I wrote how I feel or what I can do now.
exemplar: Names a specific learning experience with clear context
Events are in sequence with time connectors (first, next, finally)
Uses past-tense verbs consistently
Includes a personal detail or feeling and ends with what the writer can do now
Content is the writer's own experience, so there is no single correct story

support.clue: Choose one skill, such as riding a bike, cooking a dish, or using a new app. Think about the steps from not knowing to knowing.
support.frame: One time I learned to ______. At first, I ______. Then ______ helped me by ______. Next, I ______. Finally, ______. Now I can ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different experience. “One time I learned to whistle. At first, I only blew air and no sound came out. Then my cousin showed me how to shape my lips. Next, I practiced every evening. Finally, I made a clear sound. Now I can whistle a whole song.” Notice the first, next, and finally words, and how the story ends with what the writer can do now. Tell your story the same way.

items.stem: Retell this story from Tobias's point of view, using “I.” Include the main events in order, and tell what Tobias thinks and feels at important moments.

checklist: I told the story as Tobias, using I and my.
I included the main events in the correct order.
I described Tobias's thoughts and feelings at two or more moments.
I used time words and past-tense verbs.
exemplar: Keeps the first-person point of view consistently
Retells the key events in order: sweeping, the stopped watch, the repair, Mr. Okafor's return, the invitation
Infers feelings that fit the text (eager, nervous, relieved, proud) and gives reasons
Uses time connectors and varied past-tense verbs
Paraphrases rather than copying, and adds detail that fits the story

support.clue: Think about how Tobias feels each morning, when he opens the watch, and when Mr. Okafor asks, “Who did this?” The text does not say every feeling, so use clues from what he does.
support.frame: Every morning, I ______. I wanted to ______, but ______. One afternoon, ______. I felt ______ because ______. After I ______, ______. When Mr. Okafor came back, I ______. At the end, I felt ______ because ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different story. “Every day, I carried water to the garden. I wanted to plant seeds, but the gardener told me to wait. One morning, I found a loose seedling in the rain. I felt worried because it might die, so I placed it in soil. When the gardener saw it, I expected a scolding. Instead, she smiled. I felt proud because she trusted me.” Notice the I voice, the order of events, and feelings with reasons. Retell the clock shop story the same way.

items.stem: Samir says, “The more water a bean plant gets, the taller it grows.” Write a scientific argument about whether the data support Samir's claim. State your position, use evidence from the table, and explain your reasoning, including what the data show about 80 mL.

checklist: I said whether the data fully support, partly support, or do not support Samir's claim.
I used at least three numbers from the table as evidence.
I explained what the data show about 40 mL and 80 mL.
I gave a reason why too much water could affect a plant.
I used science words and connecting words such as however and in contrast.
exemplar: Takes a clear position that the claim is only partly supported
Cites precise data in context (2.1 cm at 0 mL, 14.6 cm at 20 mL, 15.1 cm at 40 mL, 8.3 cm at 80 mL)
Recognizes the trend: the height rises, levels off, and then falls
Gives scientific reasoning, such as too much water can harm roots, which also need air
Mentions the same soil, light, and temperature as a reason to trust the comparison, and uses contrast language

support.clue: Read down the table from 0 mL to 80 mL. Where does the height keep going up, where does it slow down, and where does it go down? Think about whether more is always better.
support.frame: The data ______ Samir's claim. From 0 mL to ______ mL, the height ______ from ______ to ______. However, at ______ mL, the height ______. This suggests that ______. A possible reason is ______. Therefore, ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different claim. “The data only partly support Mia's claim that more fertilizer is always better for tomato plants. From 0 g to 5 g, the average mass of tomatoes rose from 90 g to 160 g. However, at 20 g, it fell to 70 g. This suggests that too much fertilizer can harm the plant. A possible reason is that strong fertilizer can damage the roots. Therefore, there is a best amount in the middle.” Notice the position, the numbers, the contrast, and the reason. Evaluate Samir's claim the same way.

facts: Too much water fills the spaces in soil that hold air, and roots need oxygen from air, so overwatering can damage roots.
Table averages are invented data supplied in the stimulus.
Too much fertilizer can damage plant roots.

items.stem: The city council is asking young people to share their opinions. Write a short speech to read to your classmates that says whether the city should keep the old station or replace it with apartments. Give two reasons and ask your classmates to vote.

checklist: I told my opinion clearly.
I gave two reasons from the table.
I used because, also, or for example.
I ended by asking my classmates to vote.
exemplar: States a clear opinion in an opening that greets the audience
Gives at least two reasons that use facts from the table (history and visitors, homes for 200 families, or cost)
Uses opinion language and connectors (I think, because, also)
Closes by asking classmates to vote for the opinion
Uses a friendly, clear tone suited to a speech to classmates

support.clue: Read both rows. For the choice you pick, find two facts that make it a good idea. Think about people, history, and cost.
support.frame: Good morning, everyone. I think the city should ______ because ______. Also, ______. For example, ______. Please vote to ______. Thank you.
support.model: Mentor example about a different issue. “Good morning, everyone. I think our school should keep the old oak tree because it gives shade to students. Also, many classes use it for outdoor reading. For example, last spring, three classes read under it. Please vote to keep the tree. Thank you.” Notice the opinion, the two reasons, and the call to vote. Write your speech the same way.

facts: All details about the station and the apartments (1912, costs, 200 families) are fictional facts supplied in the table.
